passage:
At the community centre canteen, Bidisha, an engineer who kept wondering about data work, opened a notebook and a list of questions. She had promised herself to talk to four people who did the job daily, not to read glossy adverts.

Anand, an analyst, described his typical Tuesday: cleaning messy spreadsheets, meetings about what a chart should say, and very little glamour. The second, a woman from the bank, explained how she had moved in through a short certificate. A third spoke about the range of pay at the start. The fourth said, "Ask to see a real dataset."

Bidisha filled six pages. By the time she left, the job she had imagined was replaced by a more honest one, and she liked it more than before.

What was Bidisha feeling as she left the canteen?
qa.a: Bidisha felt encouraged and a little relieved, since the honest picture of the work made her like it more than the glossy one.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do next after these four conversations, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could try a small task on a real dataset, because doing some of the work shows whether the daily reality suits her.

qa.q: How might Anand see Bidisha's questions about his Tuesday?
qa.a: Anand may enjoy describing the plain truth of the job, since Bidisha seems to want honesty instead of an impressive story.

grounding: An engineer curious about data analysis speaks to four people in the field about daily tasks, pay and entry paths.

passage:
Dear Chinmay Sir,
You suggested I talk to people in data analysis before deciding anything, so here's what I did this month.
I spoke to four people. Mahesh, a data analyst at a retail company, spends most of his day cleaning messy data and writing queries, not making charts. Leena at a hospital research team said the hardest part is explaining numbers to doctors. Tariq, at a start-up, said pay ranges are wide and depend a lot on which tools you know. Gauri, who switched from mechanical engineering like me, said her entry path was one internal project and a year of evening courses.
Nobody's day sounded like the glossy job ads. Honestly, that made me more interested, not less. I liked the cleaning-data part more than I expected.
Could we meet next week to talk about which courses would make sense?
Parveen

qa.q: How did Parveen feel after hearing that the days didn't match the job ads?
qa.a: Parveen felt more interested and curious, not put off, and even liked the idea of cleaning data.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do before choosing courses?
qa.a: Parveen could try a small data-cleaning task on a public dataset, to test that interest with real work before committing.

qa.q: How might Chinmay Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Chinmay Sir might feel pleased that the advice was followed so thoroughly and that Parveen now has real information to plan with.

grounding: Shows an engineer curious about data analysis talking to four people in the field about daily work, pay and entry paths instead of relying on job ads.

passage:
"Ganga, you asked how I, Jyoti, decided on data analysis. Well, I didn't decide anything first. I asked.
I was a civil engineer at a construction firm, bored with site reports but good with spreadsheets. Every job ad for data roles looked exciting: dashboards, big decisions, cool offices. I didn't trust them.
So I found four people through my college alumni group and asked each for twenty minutes. What do you actually do all day? What did it take to get in? How does pay compare with engineering?
The answers were so different. One spent all day fixing broken data. One mostly sat in meetings. One said starting pay was lower than mine. One got in through an internal move at her company.
After those four calls I knew more than after four months of reading ads. And I knew I still wanted it, but for real reasons."

qa.q: Where did Jyoti find the four people?
qa.a: Jyoti found them through the college alumni group.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel about the job ads before the calls?
qa.a: Jyoti felt excited by them but also doubtful, not trusting how exciting they looked.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti do after the four calls?
qa.a: Jyoti could ask one of the four whether a small project or internal move is possible, turning what was learned into a first real step.

qa.q: How might the person who got in through an internal move see Jyoti's question?
qa.a: That person may feel glad to share an honest route and useful, since Jyoti asked about real work, not just the glamour.

grounding: Shows an engineer exploring data analysis by asking four people in the field about daily tasks, pay and entry paths instead of trusting job ads.
